records.source: Ἐν ἐκείνῃ τῇ ὥρᾳ προσῆλθον οἱ μαθηταὶ τῷ Ἰησοῦ λέγοντες· Τίς ἄρα μείζων ἐστὶν ἐν τῇ βασιλείᾳ τῶν οὐρανῶν;
records.gloss: In that the hour came the disciples to the Jesus saying, Who then greater is in the kingdom of the heavens?
pieces: Just then the disciples came to Jesus with a question: "So who ranks highest in the kingdom of heaven?"

L.1: At that hour the disciples came to Jesus, saying, "Who then is greatest in the kingdom of the heavens?"

R.1: At that time the followers came to Jesus and asked, "Who is the most important person in the kingdom of heaven?"

decisions.choice: at that hour: the question follows the talk of the temple tax (17:24-27)
decisions.reason: Matthew joins the scenes closely. Jesus has just spoken of the sons of the king as free; the disciples now ask about rank in the kingdom.

decisions.choice: greater: the comparative form used for "greatest"
decisions.reason: The Greek of the time often used the comparative where a superlative is meant. The disciples ask who will rank first (compare 20:20-28).

decisions.choice: then: so, in that case, drawing on what has gone before
decisions.reason: The small word marks the question as following from something already said, perhaps Peter's place in 16:18-19 and 17:1. It does not mark time.

decisions.choice: the kingdom of the heavens (L); the kingdom of heaven (B, R)
decisions.reason: As in 3:2, Literal keeps the plural and Balanced and Readable use the familiar form.

decisions.choice: the most important person
decisions.reason: Readable says what "greatest" means here: the one with the highest rank.

records.heading: Who is greatest in the kingdom

records.source: καὶ προσκαλεσάμενος παιδίον ἔστησεν αὐτὸ ἐν μέσῳ αὐτῶν καὶ εἶπεν· Ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν, ἐὰν μὴ στραφῆτε καὶ γένησθε ὡς τὰ παιδία, οὐ μὴ εἰσέλθητε εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τῶν οὐρανῶν.
records.gloss: And having called a child he set it in midst of them \v 3 and said, Truly I say to you, if not you turn and become as the children, not not you will enter into the kingdom of the heavens.
pieces: He called a little child over and stood the child among them.
Then {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said, "Truly I tell you, if you do not turn around and become like children, you will not get into the kingdom of heaven at all.

L.2: And calling a child to [{{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}], {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} set it in [the] middle of them
L.3: and said, "Truly I tell you, unless you turn and become like the children, you will never enter the kingdom of the heavens.

R.2: Jesus called a little child to come over to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}. He had the child stand among them.
R.3: Then {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said, "I tell you the truth, you must change and become like little children. If you do not, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven.

decisions.choice: turn: change the direction of your life
decisions.reason: The verb means to turn. Here it means a change of heart and ways, away from the wish to be great.

decisions.choice: become like children: in their lowly place, not in their innocence
decisions.reason: Verse 4 explains the comparison: a child humbles himself. A child had no rank or power and depended on others. The point answers the disciples' question about rank.

decisions.choice: you will never enter: a strong double negative
decisions.reason: The Greek uses two negatives together to make the denial as strong as possible. Those who seek rank are not merely low in the kingdom; they are outside it.

decisions.choice: the speech that begins here runs to 18:20
decisions.reason: Jesus's fourth long speech in Matthew begins here. After Peter's question in 18:21 it goes on to the end of the chapter.

decisions.choice: Truly I tell you (L, B); I tell you the truth (R)
decisions.reason: As in 5:18, the solemn opening is given in the same words at each level.

decisions.choice: the quotation opens here and closes at the end of 18:20
alternatives: closing and reopening the quotation at each sentence
decisions.reason: Verses 3-20 are one speech, so the quotation marks stay open to its end. Jesus speaks again from 18:22 to 18:35.

decisions.choice: Jesus
decisions.reason: Readable names Jesus at the start of the scene.

records.source: ὅστις οὖν ταπεινώσει ἑαυτὸν ὡς τὸ παιδίον τοῦτο, οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ μείζων ἐν τῇ βασιλείᾳ τῶν οὐρανῶν·
records.gloss: Whoever therefore will humble himself as the child this, he is the greater in the kingdom of the heavens;
pieces: So the greatest in the kingdom of heaven is anyone who takes a low place, as this child does.

L.4: Whoever therefore humbles {{gender:themselves|himself}} like this child, {{gender:that person|he}} is the greatest in the kingdom of the heavens;

R.4: The most important person in the kingdom of heaven is the one who stops trying to be important and becomes humble like this child.

decisions.choice: humbles himself: takes a low place of his own will
decisions.reason: The verb means to make low. A child had no standing in the society of the time; the disciple chooses that low place instead of seeking rank (23:12).

decisions.choice: like this child: as low as this child, not as humble as this child feels
alternatives: with the humble attitude of a child
decisions.reason: A child does not humble himself by choice. The comparison is with the child's position: the disciple makes himself as lowly as a child already is.

decisions.choice: the greatest: true greatness turns the disciples' idea of rank upside down
alternatives: a fixed order of rank in heaven
decisions.reason: Jesus answers their question, but not as they expected. The same reversal comes in 20:26-27.

decisions.choice: {{gender:themselves|himself}}; {{gender:that person|he}}
decisions.reason: The saying is for anyone, so the inclusive form is the default.

decisions.choice: takes a low place (B); stops trying to be important and becomes humble (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what humbling oneself means here, following the meaning decisions.

records.source: καὶ ὃς ἐὰν δέξηται ἓν παιδίον τοιοῦτο ἐπὶ τῷ ὀνόματί μου, ἐμὲ δέχεται.
records.gloss: And whoever if receives one child such in the name of me, me receives.
pieces: And when someone welcomes a child like this for {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} sake, it is {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} they welcome.

L.5: And whoever receives one such child in {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} name receives {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}.

R.5: And when people welcome a child like this because of {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, they are welcoming {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}.

decisions.choice: in my name: because of me, as one who belongs to me
decisions.reason: The phrase gives the reason for the welcome. The child is received for Jesus's sake (compare 10:40-42).

decisions.choice: one such child: a real child, and those who are lowly like one
decisions.reason: The child stands in front of them, but "such" points also to disciples who have made themselves low (18:4). Verse 6 moves on to "these little ones who believe in me".

decisions.choice: receive: welcome as a guest and care for
decisions.reason: The verb is used of welcoming people into one's home (10:14, 40). Caring for the lowly is caring for Jesus himself (25:40).

decisions.choice: for my sake (B); because of me (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what the phrase means, following the meaning decision. Literal keeps "in my name".

records.source: Ὃς δ’ ἂν σκανδαλίσῃ ἕνα τῶν μικρῶν τούτων τῶν πιστευόντων εἰς ἐμέ, συμφέρει αὐτῷ ἵνα κρεμασθῇ μύλος ὀνικὸς εἰς τὸν τράχηλον αὐτοῦ καὶ καταποντισθῇ ἐν τῷ πελάγει τῆς θαλάσσης.
records.gloss: Whoever but if causes to stumble one of the little ones these the believing in me, it is better for him that be hung a millstone of a donkey around the neck of him and he be drowned in the depth of the sea.
pieces: But if anyone leads into sin one of these little ones who believe in {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, that person would be better off sunk far out at sea with a great millstone fastened around their neck.

L.6: But whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} to stumble, it would be better for {{gender:them|him}} to have a donkey's millstone hung around {{gender:their|his}} neck and to be drowned in the depth of the sea.

R.6: These little ones believe in {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}. If anyone makes one of them sin, it would be better for that person to be thrown into the deep sea with a huge stone tied around their neck.

decisions.choice: causes to stumble: leads into sin, so as to fall away from faith
decisions.reason: As in 5:29, the verb pictures a trap or a stone that trips someone. Here it means leading a believer into sin or away from following Jesus.

decisions.choice: these little ones who believe in me: Jesus's disciples, lowly in the world's eyes
decisions.reason: "Who believe in me" shows that believers are meant, as in 10:42. The child of 18:2 stands for them.

decisions.choice: a donkey's millstone: the heavy upper stone of a mill turned by a donkey
decisions.reason: Most grinding was done with small stones turned by hand. This is the large stone of a mill worked by an animal, far too heavy to swim with.

decisions.choice: it would be better for him: what awaits him is worse than drowning
alternatives: a punishment the church should carry out
decisions.reason: Jesus does not command anyone to be drowned. He says that a terrible death would be better than the judgment that faces one who ruins a believer.

decisions.choice: {{gender:them|him}}; {{gender:their|his}}
decisions.reason: The warning is for anyone, so the inclusive form is the default.

decisions.choice: leads into sin (B); makes one of them sin (R)
decisions.reason: As in 5:29, Balanced and Readable say what the picture means.

decisions.choice: These little ones believe in me. (first)
alternatives: one of these little ones who believe in me
decisions.reason: Readable says first who the little ones are, then gives the warning.

records.heading: Woe to those who trip up the little ones

records.source: οὐαὶ τῷ κόσμῳ ἀπὸ τῶν σκανδάλων· ἀνάγκη γὰρ ἐλθεῖν τὰ σκάνδαλα, πλὴν οὐαὶ τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ δι’ οὗ τὸ σκάνδαλον ἔρχεται.
records.gloss: Woe to the world because of the stumbling blocks; necessary for to come the stumbling blocks, but woe to the man through whom the stumbling block comes.
pieces: Woe to the world for the snares that trip people into sin! Such snares are sure to come, but woe to anyone who brings one about!

L.7: Woe to the world because of the causes of stumbling! For it is necessary that causes of stumbling come, but woe to the {{gender:person|man}} through whom the cause of stumbling comes!

R.7: How terrible it will be for the people of the world because of the things that make people sin! These things will surely happen. But how terrible it will be for anyone who causes them!

decisions.choice: woe: a cry of grief and warning over coming judgment
decisions.reason: As in 11:21, the word both mourns and warns. Jesus speaks of the judgment that will fall.

decisions.choice: the world: humankind, which suffers from the things that lead to sin
decisions.reason: Here the world is the human race. The first woe pities it; the second falls on the one through whom the harm comes.

decisions.choice: necessary: such things are bound to happen in a fallen world
decisions.reason: That snares will come does not excuse the one who sets them. Matthew holds both sides together, as with Judas (26:24).

decisions.choice: stumbling blocks: whatever trips a person into sin
decisions.reason: The noun is related to the verb of 18:6. It first meant the trigger of a trap.

decisions.choice: Woe
decisions.reason: As in 11:21, Literal and Balanced keep the old word for a cry of judgment. Readable says what it means.

decisions.choice: {{gender:person|man}}
decisions.reason: The warning is for anyone, so the inclusive form is the default. Balanced and Readable say "anyone".

decisions.choice: the people of the world
decisions.reason: Readable says that the world here means people.

records.source: Εἰ δὲ ἡ χείρ σου ἢ ὁ πούς σου σκανδαλίζει σε, ἔκκοψον αὐτὸν καὶ βάλε ἀπὸ σοῦ· καλόν σοί ἐστιν εἰσελθεῖν εἰς τὴν ζωὴν κυλλὸν ἢ χωλόν, ἢ δύο χεῖρας ἢ δύο πόδας ἔχοντα βληθῆναι εἰς τὸ πῦρ τὸ αἰώνιον.
records.gloss: If but the hand of you or the foot of you causes to stumble you, cut off it and throw from you; good for you it is to enter into the life crippled or lame, than two hands or two feet having to be thrown into the fire the eternal.
pieces: If your hand or your foot leads you into sin, cut it off and get rid of it. You are better off entering life maimed or lame than keeping both hands or both feet and being thrown into the eternal fire.

L.8: And if your hand or your foot causes you to stumble, cut it off and throw [it] away from you; it is better for you to enter life crippled or lame than to have two hands or two feet and be thrown into the eternal fire.

R.8: If your hand or your foot makes you sin, cut it off and throw it away. It is better to have life with God with only one hand or one foot than to have two hands and two feet and be thrown into the eternal fire.

decisions.choice: cut off: overstatement that demands drastic action against sin
alternatives: a command to harm the body
decisions.reason: As in 5:29-30, Jesus uses deliberate overstatement. The point is to deal ruthlessly with whatever leads to sin, because the stakes are eternal.

decisions.choice: enter life: enter eternal life in the kingdom
alternatives: go on living in this world
decisions.reason: Life is set against the eternal fire. Matthew uses "enter life" and "enter the kingdom" for the same thing (19:17, 23).

decisions.choice: the eternal fire: the fire of final judgment, which does not end
alternatives: a fire that lasts a long time
decisions.reason: The word means belonging to the age to come and so without end. Matthew uses the same phrase in 25:41 and sets eternal punishment against eternal life in 25:46.

decisions.choice: causes you to stumble: leads you into sin
decisions.reason: As in 5:29. In 18:6-7 others cause the stumbling; here a person's own hand or foot does.

decisions.choice: leads you into sin (B); makes you sin (R)
decisions.reason: As in 5:29-30, Balanced and Readable say what the picture means.

decisions.choice: have life with God
decisions.reason: Readable says what life is meant, following the meaning decision.

records.source: καὶ εἰ ὁ ὀφθαλμός σου σκανδαλίζει σε, ἔξελε αὐτὸν καὶ βάλε ἀπὸ σοῦ· καλόν σοί ἐστιν μονόφθαλμον εἰς τὴν ζωὴν εἰσελθεῖν, ἢ δύο ὀφθαλμοὺς ἔχοντα βληθῆναι εἰς τὴν γέενναν τοῦ πυρός.
records.gloss: And if the eye of you causes to stumble you, tear out it and throw from you; good for you it is one-eyed into the life to enter, than two eyes having to be thrown into the Gehenna of the fire.
pieces: And if your eye leads you into sin, pull it out and get rid of it. You are better off entering life with one eye than keeping both eyes and being thrown into the fire of hell.

L.9: And if your eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and throw [it] away from you; it is better for you to enter life with one eye than to have two eyes and be thrown into the Gehenna of fire.

R.9: If your eye makes you sin, pull it out and throw it away. It is better to have life with God with only one eye than to have two eyes and be thrown into the fire of hell.

decisions.choice: tear out: overstatement that demands drastic action against sin
alternatives: a command to harm the body
decisions.reason: As in 5:29 and 18:8.

decisions.choice: the Gehenna of fire: the place of final judgment
decisions.reason: As in 5:22, Gehenna was the valley of Hinnom by Jerusalem, whose name became a name for the fire of God's judgment. Here it stands in place of "the eternal fire" of 18:8.

decisions.choice: Gehenna (L); hell (B, R)
decisions.reason: As in 5:22 and 5:29, Literal keeps the place name and Balanced and Readable use the word for the place of final judgment.

decisions.choice: leads you into sin (B); makes you sin (R)
decisions.reason: As in 18:8.

records.source: Ὁρᾶτε μὴ καταφρονήσητε ἑνὸς τῶν μικρῶν τούτων, λέγω γὰρ ὑμῖν ὅτι οἱ ἄγγελοι αὐτῶν ἐν οὐρανοῖς διὰ παντὸς βλέπουσι τὸ πρόσωπον τοῦ πατρός μου τοῦ ἐν οὐρανοῖς.
records.gloss: See not you despise one of the little ones these, I say for to you that the angels of them in heavens continually see the face of the Father of me the in heavens.
pieces: Take care never to look down on a single one of these little ones. I tell you, their angels in heaven stand always in the presence of {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} Father in heaven.

L.10: See that you do not despise one of these little ones, for I tell you that their angels in [the] heavens always see the face of {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} Father who [is] in [the] heavens.

R.10: Be careful that you do not think any of these little ones are unimportant. I tell you, they have angels in heaven who are always with {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} Father in heaven.

decisions.choice: their angels: angels who care for the little ones
decisions.reason: Scripture speaks of angels sent to guard God's people (Psalm 91:11; Hebrews 1:14), and Acts 12:15 shows the belief that a person had an angel. The verse does not say more about how this is arranged.

decisions.choice: see the face: stand in the presence, with access to the king
decisions.reason: Those who saw the king's face were his closest servants, who could come before him at any time (2 Samuel 14:24; Esther 1:14). The little ones may seem of no account, but their angels have the Father's ear.

decisions.choice: no verse 11, the reading of the SBLGNT
alternatives: "For the Son of Man came to save the lost," added as verse 11 in many manuscripts
decisions.reason: Early manuscripts go straight from verse 10 to verse 12. Many later ones add a verse very like Luke 19:10, probably taken from there to lead into the parable of the lost sheep. Older translations print it as verse 11. Reviewers should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: despise: treat as worthless, look down on
decisions.reason: The verb means to think little of someone. The little ones are easy to overlook because they have no rank.

decisions.choice: stand always in the presence of (B); are always with (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what the picture means, following the meaning decision.

records.heading: The Father seeks the sheep that strays

records.source: τί ὑμῖν δοκεῖ;
records.gloss: What to you seems?
pieces: Tell me what you think.

decisions.choice: what do you think: an invitation to judge the case that follows
alternatives: a request for opinions in general
decisions.reason: Jesus asks his hearers to judge from what they know, as in 17:25 and 21:28.

decisions.choice: Tell me what you think (B); Think about this (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable turn the question into an invitation, which is how it works.

records.source: ἐὰν γένηταί τινι ἀνθρώπῳ ἑκατὸν πρόβατα καὶ πλανηθῇ ἓν ἐξ αὐτῶν, οὐχὶ ἀφήσει τὰ ἐνενήκοντα ἐννέα ἐπὶ τὰ ὄρη καὶ πορευθεὶς ζητεῖ τὸ πλανώμενον;
records.gloss: If there be to any man a hundred sheep and goes astray one of them, not will he leave the ninety nine on the mountains and having gone seek the straying?
pieces: Suppose someone owns a hundred sheep, and one of them wanders off. Will the owner not leave the ninety-nine on the hillsides and set out to search for the one that strayed?

L.12: If a man has a hundred sheep and one of them goes astray, will he not leave the ninety-nine on the mountains and go and look for the one that is straying?

R.12: Suppose someone has a hundred sheep and one of them wanders away. The owner will leave the other ninety-nine sheep on the hills and go to look for the lost one.

decisions.choice: will he not leave: a question that expects "yes"
decisions.reason: The Greek form shows that any owner would go looking. Leaving the flock on the open hills was a risk worth taking for the one lost sheep.

decisions.choice: the straying sheep: Ezekiel 34:11-16
decisions.reason: In Ezekiel God promises to seek out his scattered sheep himself and bring back the strays. Luke 15:3-7 tells the same parable about sinners who repent; here it is about a believer who wanders.

decisions.choice: go astray: wander away and be lost
decisions.reason: The verb means to wander off the right way, and is used of being led into error (24:4-5, 11). The sheep is the little one who has been led to stumble (18:6).

decisions.choice: a man (L); someone, the owner (B, R), with no gender or deity_pronoun span
decisions.reason: The owner is a figure in a picture, so the pronouns take no span. Balanced and Readable avoid naming a man, since the point is what any owner would do.

decisions.choice: a statement instead of a question
alternatives: Will he not leave the ninety-nine?
decisions.reason: The question expects "yes"; Readable gives the answer.

decisions.choice: hillsides (B); hills (R)
decisions.reason: The word covers hill country as well as mountains, where sheep were grazed.

records.source: καὶ ἐὰν γένηται εὑρεῖν αὐτό, ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν ὅτι χαίρει ἐπ’ αὐτῷ μᾶλλον ἢ ἐπὶ τοῖς ἐνενήκοντα ἐννέα τοῖς μὴ πεπλανημένοις.
records.gloss: And if it happens to find it, truly I say to you that he rejoices over it more than over the ninety nine the not having gone astray.
pieces: And if the owner does find it, truly I tell you, that one sheep brings more delight than the ninety-nine that never wandered off.

L.13: And if he happens to find it, truly I tell you that he rejoices over it more than over the ninety-nine that did not go astray.

R.13: And if the owner finds it, I tell you the truth, the owner is happier about that one sheep than about the ninety-nine that did not wander away.

decisions.choice: if he happens to find it: finding is not certain
decisions.reason: The words leave room for the search to fail. That makes the joy of finding greater, and it fits the warning of 18:14 that a little one could perish.

decisions.choice: rejoices more: the joy of finding what was lost
decisions.reason: The others are not loved less. The joy over the one that is found back is the stronger feeling of the moment.

decisions.choice: truly I tell you (L, B); I tell you the truth (R)
decisions.reason: As in 18:3.

decisions.choice: that one sheep brings more delight
decisions.reason: Balanced makes the sheep the subject to keep the sentence short.

records.source: οὕτως οὐκ ἔστιν θέλημα ἔμπροσθεν τοῦ πατρὸς ὑμῶν τοῦ ἐν οὐρανοῖς ἵνα ἀπόληται ἓν τῶν μικρῶν τούτων.
records.gloss: So not it is will before the Father of you the in heavens that should perish one of the little ones these.
pieces: So too, your Father in heaven does not wish to lose even one of these little ones.

L.14: So it is not [the] will before your Father who [is] in [the] heavens that one of these little ones should perish.

R.14: Your Father in heaven is like that. He does not want even one of these little ones to be lost.

decisions.choice: the will before your Father: your Father's will
alternatives: a will set before the Father by someone else
decisions.reason: Speaking of the will "before" God was a respectful way of speaking of God's will, as in 11:26.

decisions.choice: perish: be lost and ruined for ever
decisions.reason: The verb is used of the lost sheep (10:6; 15:24) and of final ruin (10:28). The little one who strays could be lost for good.

decisions.choice: your Father, the reading of the SBLGNT
alternatives: my Father, the reading of some manuscripts
decisions.reason: Some manuscripts read "my Father", as in 18:10 and 18:19. Reviewers should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: so: the parable applied
decisions.reason: As the owner seeks the stray, so the Father wants none of the little ones lost. The disciples are to share that will (18:10).

decisions.choice: does not wish to lose (B); does not want to be lost (R)
alternatives: it is not the will that should perish
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say the same thing with a verb; Literal keeps "will".

decisions.choice: Your Father in heaven is like that.
decisions.reason: Readable spells out the comparison with the owner.

records.source: Ἐὰν δὲ ἁμαρτήσῃ εἰς σὲ ὁ ἀδελφός σου, ὕπαγε ἔλεγξον αὐτὸν μεταξὺ σοῦ καὶ αὐτοῦ μόνου.
records.gloss: If but sins against you the brother of you, go reprove him between you and him alone.
pieces: If {{gender:a brother or sister|your brother}} sins against you, go and confront {{gender:them|him}} about it, with only the two of you present.

L.15: And if {{gender:your brother or sister|your brother}} sins against you, go, show {{gender:them|him}} [the] fault between you and {{gender:them|him}} alone.

R.15: If {{gender:a brother or sister|your brother}} in God's family sins against you, go and talk to {{gender:them|him}} alone. Show {{gender:them|him}} what {{gender:they|he}} did wrong.

decisions.choice: brother: a fellow member of the community of disciples, man or woman
decisions.reason: As in 5:22-24 and 12:49-50, a brother is one who belongs to Jesus's family of disciples. The teaching applies to women as well as men.

decisions.choice: sins against you, the reading of the SBLGNT
alternatives: sins, without "against you", the reading of some early manuscripts
decisions.reason: Some important early manuscripts lack "against you". Without it, the teaching covers any sin of a fellow disciple, not only a wrong done to you. The words may have been added from 18:21, or dropped by a copyist. Reviewers should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: show the fault: bring the wrong into the open so that it is admitted
decisions.reason: The verb means to expose or convince. The aim is to win the person back (18:15), as in Leviticus 19:17.

decisions.choice: Leviticus 19:17: rebuke your neighbor, and do not hate him
decisions.reason: The law told Israel to correct a neighbor openly rather than nurse hatred in the heart.

decisions.choice: {{gender:a brother or sister|your brother}}; {{gender:them|him}}
decisions.reason: The teaching covers women and men, so the inclusive form is the default.

decisions.choice: in God's family
decisions.reason: Readable says that a fellow believer is meant.

records.heading: When a fellow believer sins against you

records.source: ἐάν σου ἀκούσῃ, ἐκέρδησας τὸν ἀδελφόν σου·
records.gloss: If you he hears, you have gained the brother of you;
pieces: If {{gender:they|he}} will listen to you, you have won {{gender:your brother or sister|your brother}} back.

L.15: If {{gender:they|he}} will listen to you, you have gained {{gender:your brother or sister|your brother}};

R.15: Maybe {{gender:they|he}} will listen to you. Then you have won {{gender:your brother or sister|your brother}} back.

decisions.choice: gained: won back to God and to the community
decisions.reason: The verb is a word from trade. Here what is gained is the person, brought back from the path of sin, like the sheep in 18:13.

decisions.choice: listen: heed, accept the correction
decisions.reason: To listen here is to take the correction to heart and put the wrong right.

decisions.choice: will listen
decisions.reason: The helping verb lets the gender setting change the pronoun without changing the verb.

decisions.choice: won back
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what the gain is.

records.source: ἐὰν δὲ μὴ ἀκούσῃ, παράλαβε μετὰ σοῦ ἔτι ἕνα ἢ δύο, ἵνα ἐπὶ στόματος δύο μαρτύρων ἢ τριῶν σταθῇ πᾶν ῥῆμα·
records.gloss: If but not he hears, take with you yet one or two, that on mouth of two witnesses or three may be established every word;
pieces: If {{gender:they|he}} still will not listen, go back with one or two others, so that 'every charge may be settled on the word of two or three witnesses.'

L.16: But if {{gender:they|he}} will not listen, take one or two more with you, so that 'by [the] mouth of two or three witnesses every word may be established.'

R.16: If {{gender:they|he}} will still not listen, take one or two other people with you. The Scriptures say, 'Every charge must be proved by two or three witnesses.'

decisions.choice: Deuteronomy 19:15: two or three witnesses
decisions.reason: The law said that a charge must be confirmed by two or three witnesses. Paul uses the same rule in 2 Corinthians 13:1.

decisions.choice: every word: every matter, every charge
decisions.reason: Like the Hebrew word it follows, the word can mean a matter or case as well as a word.

decisions.choice: so that: the others confirm what is said and help win the person
alternatives: the others serve only as a court
decisions.reason: The witnesses make sure the matter is fairly heard. They may also add their voice to the call to put things right.

decisions.choice: The Scriptures say
decisions.reason: Readable says that the words come from the law.

decisions.choice: {{gender:they|he}}
decisions.reason: As in 18:15.

records.source: ἐὰν δὲ παρακούσῃ αὐτῶν, εἰπὸν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ· ἐὰν δὲ καὶ τῆς ἐκκλησίας παρακούσῃ, ἔστω σοι ὥσπερ ὁ ἐθνικὸς καὶ ὁ τελώνης.
records.gloss: If but he refuses to hear them, tell to the church; if but also the church he refuses to hear, let him be to you as the Gentile and the tax collector.
pieces: If {{gender:they|he}} will not hear them either, bring the matter before the church. And if {{gender:they|he}} will not hear the church either, regard {{gender:them|him}} as an outsider, like a Gentile or a tax collector.

L.17: And if {{gender:they|he}} will not heed them, tell [it] to the church; and if {{gender:they|he}} will not heed even the church, let {{gender:them|him}} be to you like the Gentile and the tax collector.

R.17: If {{gender:they|he}} will not listen to them, tell the whole church. If {{gender:they|he}} will not listen even to the church, treat {{gender:them|him}} like someone who does not know God, or like a tax collector.

decisions.choice: the church: the gathered community of Jesus's disciples
decisions.reason: The word means an assembly. Jesus used it in 16:18 of the community he would build; here it is the local gathering of believers.

decisions.choice: the Gentile and the tax collector: people outside the fellowship
decisions.reason: Jews of the time kept apart from Gentiles and tax collectors at table (9:11). The one who will not repent is to be treated as outside the community. Yet Jesus himself sought out tax collectors (9:9-13; 11:19), and the parable of the sheep goes before these words.

decisions.choice: the Gentile: one outside Israel who did not worship its God
alternatives: a foreigner in a neutral sense
decisions.reason: As in 5:47 and 6:7.

decisions.choice: an outsider
decisions.reason: Balanced says what the comparison means, following the meaning decision.

decisions.choice: someone who does not know God
decisions.reason: Readable explains the word, as in 5:47.

decisions.choice: {{gender:they|he}}; {{gender:them|him}}
decisions.reason: As in 18:15.

records.source: ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν, ὅσα ἐὰν δήσητε ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς ἔσται δεδεμένα ἐν οὐρανῷ καὶ ὅσα ἐὰν λύσητε ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς ἔσται λελυμένα ἐν οὐρανῷ.
records.gloss: Truly I say to you, as many as if you bind on the earth will be having been bound in heaven, and as many as if you loose on the earth will be having been loosed in heaven.
pieces: Truly I tell you, what you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and what you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven.

L.18: Truly I tell you, whatever you bind on earth will have been bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will have been loosed in heaven.

R.18: I tell you the truth, whatever you forbid on earth will be forbidden in heaven. And whatever you allow on earth will be allowed in heaven.

decisions.choice: bind and loose: decide what is forbidden and what is allowed, and so whom to hold to their sin and whom to set free
decisions.reason: Jewish teachers spoke of binding and loosing when they ruled what the law forbade or allowed. Here, after 18:15-17, it covers the church's judgment on a member who sins. Compare 16:19 and John 20:23.

decisions.choice: will have been bound: heaven's verdict stands with the church's
alternatives: heaven will afterward agree with whatever the church decides
decisions.reason: The form is a future perfect. It may mean that the church's decision follows what God has already decided, or simply that God will confirm it. The grammar does not settle the order.

decisions.choice: you: the plural, the disciples together
decisions.reason: In 16:19 the same promise is made to Peter. Here the "you" is plural, and the church of 18:17 is in view.

decisions.choice: will be bound; will be loosed, as at 16:19
alternatives: will stand bound; will stand free
decisions.reason: Balanced uses the same words as at 16:19, so readers can see it is the same promise, now given to all the disciples. Literal keeps the future perfect form.

decisions.choice: forbid; allow
decisions.reason: Readable gives the sense of the idiom, following the meaning decision.

records.source: Πάλιν ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν ὅτι ἐὰν δύο συμφωνήσωσιν ἐξ ὑμῶν ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς περὶ παντὸς πράγματος οὗ ἐὰν αἰτήσωνται, γενήσεται αὐτοῖς παρὰ τοῦ πατρός μου τοῦ ἐν οὐρανοῖς.
records.gloss: Again truly I say to you that if two agree of you on the earth about any matter which if they ask, it will be done for them by the Father of me the in heavens.
pieces: And again, truly I tell you: if two of you here on earth are of one mind about anything they ask for, it will be done for them by {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} Father in heaven.

L.19: Again, truly I tell you that if two of you agree on earth about any matter that they ask, it will be done for them by {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} Father who [is] in [the] heavens.

R.19: I tell you the truth again. Suppose two of you here on earth agree about something and ask God for it. Then {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} Father in heaven will do it for them.

decisions.choice: any matter: anything they ask, including the cases the church must judge
decisions.reason: The word can mean a legal case (1 Corinthians 6:1), which fits the setting of 18:15-18. But the promise is put broadly, about anything asked.

decisions.choice: agree: be of one mind, in harmony
decisions.reason: The verb means to sound together. The disciples ask God together, in agreement.

decisions.choice: ask God for it
decisions.reason: Readable says to whom they ask.

records.source: οὗ γάρ εἰσιν δύο ἢ τρεῖς συνηγμένοι εἰς τὸ ἐμὸν ὄνομα, ἐκεῖ εἰμι ἐν μέσῳ αὐτῶν.
records.gloss: Where for are two or three gathered into the my name, there I am in midst of them.
pieces: For whenever two or three come together in {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} name, I am there among them."

L.20: For where two or three are gathered in {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} name, there I am in [the] middle of them."

R.20: When two or three people meet together because they follow {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, I am there with them."

decisions.choice: gathered in my name: meeting as those who belong to me
alternatives: meeting while saying my name aloud
decisions.reason: As in 18:5, "in my name" names the bond with Jesus. They meet as his disciples.

decisions.choice: I am there among them: the promise of Jesus's presence
decisions.reason: Matthew opens with "God with us" (1:23) and closes with "I am with you always" (28:20). Jesus promises to be with even the smallest gathering of his disciples.

decisions.choice: for: the reason the Father hears the two
decisions.reason: The Father answers their prayer because Jesus is present with those who meet in his name.

decisions.choice: because they follow me
decisions.reason: Readable says what "in my name" means here.

decisions.choice: the quotation closes here
decisions.reason: Peter's question in 18:21 breaks into the speech, so the quotation closes here and reopens at 18:22.

records.source: Τότε προσελθὼν αὐτῷ ὁ Πέτρος εἶπεν· Κύριε, ποσάκις ἁμαρτήσει εἰς ἐμὲ ὁ ἀδελφός μου καὶ ἀφήσω αὐτῷ;
records.gloss: Then having come to him the Peter said, Lord, how often will sin against me the brother of me and I will forgive him?
pieces: Then Peter came to Jesus and asked, "Lord, if {{gender:a brother or sister|my brother}} keeps on sinning against me, how many times must I forgive?

L.21: Then Peter came to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} and said, "Lord, how many times will {{gender:my brother or sister|my brother}} sin against me and I forgive {{gender:them|him}}?

R.21: Then Peter came to Jesus and asked, "Lord, suppose {{gender:a brother or sister|my brother}} in God's family sins against me again and again. How many times should I forgive {{gender:them|him}}?

decisions.choice: how many times: how often must I forgive the same person
decisions.reason: Peter asks about one person who sins against him again and again. He takes up the brother of 18:15.

decisions.choice: my brother: a fellow disciple, man or woman
decisions.reason: As in 18:15.

decisions.choice: forgive: let go of the wrong and not hold it against the person
decisions.reason: The verb means to release or let go, the word used of debts in 6:12 and 18:27.

decisions.choice: Jesus
decisions.reason: A new section begins here, so Balanced and Readable name Jesus.

decisions.choice: {{gender:a brother or sister|my brother}}; {{gender:them|him}}
decisions.reason: As in 18:15, the inclusive form is the default.

decisions.choice: the quotation opens here and closes at the end of 18:21
alternatives: closing the quotation at the end of this sentence
decisions.reason: Peter's question runs over two sentences.

records.heading: How many times to forgive

records.source: ἕως ἑπτάκις;
records.gloss: Up to seven times?
pieces: As many as seven times?"

decisions.choice: seven times: a generous number
decisions.reason: Seven is the number of fullness. Peter offers more than would usually be expected (compare Luke 17:4).

decisions.choice: Should I forgive
decisions.reason: Readable makes the short question a full sentence.

records.source: λέγει αὐτῷ ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Οὐ λέγω σοι ἕως ἑπτάκις ἀλλὰ ἕως ἑβδομηκοντάκις ἑπτά.
records.gloss: Says to him the Jesus, Not I say to you up to seven times but up to seventy times seven.
pieces: Jesus told him, "Not just up to seven times, but up to seventy-seven times.

L.22: Jesus says to him, "I do not say to you up to seven times, but up to seventy-seven times.

R.22: Jesus answered, "I tell you, not only seven times. You must forgive seventy-seven times.

decisions.choice: seventy-seven times
alternatives: seventy times seven, that is, four hundred and ninety times
decisions.reason: The Greek words can be read either way. The same words stand in the Greek Old Testament for Lamech's "seventy-seven times" in Genesis 4:24, which suggests that sense. Either way, Jesus means there is to be no limit.

decisions.choice: Genesis 4:24: Lamech's boast of revenge seventy-seven times
decisions.reason: Lamech boasted that he would be avenged seventy-seven times. Jesus turns the number of unlimited revenge into a number of unlimited forgiveness.

decisions.choice: present tense of narration (L); past (B, R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the Greek present tense of narration.

decisions.choice: the quotation opens here and closes at the end of 18:35
alternatives: closing the quotation at the end of this sentence
decisions.reason: Jesus's answer goes on into the parable of 18:23-35, which is one speech.

decisions.choice: You must forgive
decisions.reason: Readable makes the answer a full sentence.

records.source: Διὰ τοῦτο ὡμοιώθη ἡ βασιλεία τῶν οὐρανῶν ἀνθρώπῳ βασιλεῖ ὃς ἠθέλησεν συνᾶραι λόγον μετὰ τῶν δούλων αὐτοῦ·
records.gloss: Because of this has been likened the kingdom of the heavens to a man a king who wanted to settle account with the slaves of him;
pieces: That is why the kingdom of heaven is like this: a king decided it was time to go over the accounts of his servants.

L.23: Because of this, the kingdom of the heavens has been compared to a man, a king, who wanted to settle accounts with his slaves.

R.23: So this is what the kingdom of heaven is like. There was a king who decided to have his servants settle what they owed him.

decisions.choice: because of this: the parable shows why forgiveness has no limit
alternatives: a loose link with no reason given
decisions.reason: The story explains the answer to Peter: those whom God has forgiven so much must forgive others.

decisions.choice: slaves: royal slaves, who might hold high office
decisions.reason: A king's slaves could manage large sums for him, such as the taxes of a province. They were still his property and answered to him. The word is the one for a slave.

decisions.choice: has been compared: the kingdom is like the whole story
alternatives: the kingdom is like the king himself
decisions.reason: As in 13:24, the comparison is with what happens in the story, not only with its first figure.

decisions.choice: a king, with no deity_pronoun span for him in the story
decisions.reason: The king is a figure in a parable, so the pronouns for him take no span, though he stands for God (18:35).

decisions.choice: servants
decisions.reason: "Servant" in Balanced and Readable, as the style guide has it; the meaning decision (m2) keeps that they were owned, and Literal keeps "slave".

records.heading: The servant who would not forgive

records.source: ἀρξαμένου δὲ αὐτοῦ συναίρειν προσηνέχθη αὐτῷ εἷς ὀφειλέτης μυρίων ταλάντων.
records.gloss: Having begun and he to settle was brought to him one debtor of ten thousand talents.
pieces: As he began, a man was brought before him who owed him {{units:a sum no worker could earn in a hundred thousand years|ten thousand talents}}.

L.24: And when he had begun to settle, one was brought to him who was a debtor of ten thousand talents.

R.24: As he began, a servant was brought to him who owed him {{units:a sum no worker could earn in a hundred thousand years|ten thousand talents}}. No one could ever pay back that much money.

decisions.choice: ten thousand talents: a sum beyond counting
decisions.reason: A talent was a weight of silver worth about six thousand denarii, and a denarius was a laborer's pay for a day (20:2). Ten thousand talents was about sixty million days' wages, more than a laborer could earn in many lifetimes. Ten thousand was the largest number in common Greek use.

decisions.choice: was brought: he was made to come, perhaps under guard
decisions.reason: The passive suggests he did not come willingly.

decisions.choice: {{units:a sum no worker could earn in a hundred thousand years|ten thousand talents}}
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give a modern figure by default, with the original sum as the alternative. Literal keeps the talents.

decisions.choice: No one could ever pay back that much money.
decisions.reason: Readable says what the sum meant to the hearers.

records.source: μὴ ἔχοντος δὲ αὐτοῦ ἀποδοῦναι ἐκέλευσεν αὐτὸν ὁ κύριος πραθῆναι καὶ τὴν γυναῖκα καὶ τὰ τέκνα καὶ πάντα ὅσα ἔχει καὶ ἀποδοθῆναι.
records.gloss: Not having but he to pay, commanded him the master to be sold and the wife and the children and all as much as he has, and to be paid.
pieces: He had no means of paying, so his master gave orders for him to be sold, together with his wife, his children and all he owned, to pay toward the debt.

L.25: And since he did not have [the means] to pay, the master ordered him to be sold, and [his] wife and children and everything he had, and payment to be made.

R.25: The servant could not pay. So the king ordered that he be sold as a slave, along with his wife and children and everything he owned. The money would go toward paying what he owed.

decisions.choice: sold with his family: a debtor and his household could be sold into slavery
alternatives: a punishment the law of Moses required
decisions.reason: Selling a debtor and his family was known in Israel (2 Kings 4:1; Nehemiah 5:5) and across the ancient world. The sale would cover only a tiny part of such a debt.

decisions.choice: the master: the king of 18:23
decisions.reason: The word means lord or master. In the story it is the king, the slave's owner.

decisions.choice: the king
decisions.reason: Readable keeps one name for the king throughout the story.

decisions.choice: [the means]; [his]
decisions.reason: Literal brackets the words English needs.

decisions.choice: sold as a slave
decisions.reason: Readable calls the man "servant" in this parable, as the style guide has it, but keeps "slave" where the king orders him sold with his family: being sold as property is the point here (m1).

records.source: πεσὼν οὖν ὁ δοῦλος προσεκύνει αὐτῷ λέγων· Μακροθύμησον ἐπ’ ἐμοί, καὶ πάντα ἀποδώσω σοι.
records.gloss: Having fallen therefore the slave was bowing down to him saying, Be patient with me, and all I will pay to you.
pieces: At that the servant threw himself to the ground before him and pleaded, 'Give me time, and I will pay back all of it.'

L.26: So the slave fell down and was bowing before him, saying, 'Be patient with me, and I will pay you everything.'

R.26: The servant got down on his knees in front of the king and begged, 'Please be patient with me. I will pay you everything.'

decisions.choice: was bowing: bowing low before a king
decisions.reason: The verb is used for worship and also for bowing low before a ruler, as here. The tense pictures him pleading on and on.

decisions.choice: I will pay you everything: a promise he could never keep
decisions.reason: No slave could repay such a sum (18:24). He asks for time, but the king gives far more.

decisions.choice: single quotation marks
decisions.reason: The slave's words are inside Jesus's speech, so they take inner quotation marks.

decisions.choice: pleaded (B); begged (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say how he spoke, as the bowing shows.

decisions.choice: servant
decisions.reason: "Servant" in Balanced and Readable, as the style guide has it, and Literal keeps "slave".

records.source: σπλαγχνισθεὶς δὲ ὁ κύριος τοῦ δούλου ἐκείνου ἀπέλυσεν αὐτόν, καὶ τὸ δάνειον ἀφῆκεν αὐτῷ.
records.gloss: Having been moved with compassion and the master of the slave that released him, and the loan forgave him.
pieces: The master was moved with pity for that servant. He set him free and forgave him the debt.

L.27: And the master of that slave, moved with compassion, released him and forgave him the loan.

R.27: The king felt sorry for the servant. So he let him go free and forgave him the whole debt.

decisions.choice: moved with compassion: deeply moved
decisions.reason: This is the word used of Jesus's compassion for the crowds (9:36; 14:14).

decisions.choice: the loan: the debt, spoken of as money lent
decisions.reason: Whatever the slave had received from the king, the master treats it as a loan and cancels it.

decisions.choice: forgave: the same verb as Peter's question (18:21) and 18:35
decisions.reason: The master does more than the slave asked. He does not give time; he lets the whole debt go.

decisions.choice: forgave
decisions.reason: The same word is kept at every level to tie the story to Peter's question and to 18:35.

decisions.choice: the whole debt
decisions.reason: Readable says that the debt was cancelled in full, as 18:32 says.

decisions.choice: servant
decisions.reason: "Servant" in Balanced and Readable, as the style guide has it, and Literal keeps "slave".

records.source: ἐξελθὼν δὲ ὁ δοῦλος ἐκεῖνος εὗρεν ἕνα τῶν συνδούλων αὐτοῦ ὃς ὤφειλεν αὐτῷ ἑκατὸν δηνάρια, καὶ κρατήσας αὐτὸν ἔπνιγεν λέγων· Ἀπόδος εἴ τι ὀφείλεις.
records.gloss: Having gone out but the slave that found one of the fellow slaves of him who owed him a hundred denarii, and having seized him he was choking [him] saying, Pay if anything you owe.
pieces: But no sooner had that servant left than he came upon one of his fellow servants who owed him {{units:about a hundred days' wages|a hundred denarii}}. He grabbed him by the throat. 'Pay me what you owe!' he said.

L.28: But that slave went out and found one of his fellow slaves who owed him a hundred denarii, and seizing him, he began to choke [him], saying, 'Pay back whatever you owe.'

R.28: Then that servant went out and found another servant who owed him {{units:about a hundred days' wages|a hundred denarii}}. He grabbed the man and started choking him. He said, 'Pay back the money you owe me!'

decisions.choice: a hundred denarii: about a hundred days' wages
decisions.reason: A denarius was a laborer's pay for a day (20:2). A hundred denarii was a real debt, a third of a year's wages, but next to ten thousand talents it was almost nothing.

decisions.choice: pay if you owe anything: pay what you owe
alternatives: a doubt about whether he owes anything
decisions.reason: The "if" does not question the debt. It is a harsh demand for whatever is owed.

decisions.choice: was choking: began to choke him
decisions.reason: The tense pictures the action going on or beginning.

decisions.choice: {{units:about a hundred days' wages|a hundred denarii}}
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give a modern figure by default, with the original sum as the alternative. Literal keeps the denarii.

decisions.choice: fellow servants (B); another servant (R)
decisions.reason: "Servant" in Balanced and Readable, as the style guide has it; the man is in the same position as the first, owned by the king, and Literal keeps "fellow slaves".

records.source: πεσὼν οὖν ὁ σύνδουλος αὐτοῦ παρεκάλει αὐτὸν λέγων· Μακροθύμησον ἐπ’ ἐμοί, καὶ ἀποδώσω σοι.
records.gloss: Having fallen therefore the fellow slave of him was begging him saying, Be patient with me, and I will pay you.
pieces: His fellow servant dropped to the ground and pleaded with him, 'Give me time, and I will pay you back.'

L.29: So his fellow slave fell down and was begging him, saying, 'Be patient with me, and I will pay you.'

R.29: The other servant got down on his knees and begged him, 'Please be patient with me. I will pay you back.'

decisions.choice: the same plea as 18:26
decisions.reason: The words are almost those the first slave used to the king, and this debt could in fact be repaid. The echo makes the first slave's refusal plain.

decisions.choice: fell down, the reading of the SBLGNT
alternatives: fell down at his feet, and "I will pay you everything", the reading of many later manuscripts
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts add "at his feet" and "everything", making the plea match 18:26 more closely. Reviewers should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: the same words as 18:26 at each level
decisions.reason: The echo is kept so that readers hear the same plea.

decisions.choice: servant
decisions.reason: "Servant" in Balanced and Readable, as the style guide has it, and Literal keeps "slave".

records.source: ὁ δὲ οὐκ ἤθελεν, ἀλλὰ ἀπελθὼν ἔβαλεν αὐτὸν εἰς φυλακὴν ἕως οὗ ἀποδῷ τὸ ὀφειλόμενον.
records.gloss: He but not was willing, but having gone away he threw him into prison until he should pay the being owed.
pieces: But he would not hear of it. He went off and had the man put in prison until the debt was paid.

L.30: But he was not willing; instead he went and threw him into prison until he should pay what was owed.

R.30: But the first servant would not wait. He had the other man thrown into prison. He would stay there until he paid back what he owed.

decisions.choice: prison until he should pay: prison for debt
decisions.reason: As in 5:25-26, a debtor could be held until the debt was paid, often by his family or friends.

decisions.choice: threw him into prison: by legal means, as a creditor could
decisions.reason: The slave would have had the man put in prison through the officials. The wording stresses his harshness.

decisions.choice: had the man put (B); had the other man thrown (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say that he did this through others, following the meaning decision.

records.source: ἰδόντες οὖν οἱ σύνδουλοι αὐτοῦ τὰ γενόμενα ἐλυπήθησαν σφόδρα, καὶ ἐλθόντες διεσάφησαν τῷ κυρίῳ ἑαυτῶν πάντα τὰ γενόμενα.
records.gloss: Having seen therefore the fellow slaves of him the things having happened they were grieved greatly, and having come they explained to the master of themselves all the things having happened.
pieces: When the other servants saw what had taken place, they were deeply upset. They went to their master and told him the whole story.

L.31: So when his fellow slaves saw what had happened, they were deeply distressed, and they went and reported to their master all that had happened.

R.31: The other servants saw what happened, and it made them very upset. So they went and told the king everything.

decisions.choice: deeply distressed: grieved and upset
decisions.reason: The verb means to be grieved or pained. They are troubled at the cruelty they have seen.

decisions.choice: reported: explained in full
decisions.reason: The verb means to make clear. They give the master the whole account.

decisions.choice: the king
decisions.reason: As in 18:25.

decisions.choice: servants
decisions.reason: "Servant" in Balanced and Readable, as the style guide has it, and Literal keeps "slave".

records.source: τότε προσκαλεσάμενος αὐτὸν ὁ κύριος αὐτοῦ λέγει αὐτῷ· Δοῦλε πονηρέ, πᾶσαν τὴν ὀφειλὴν ἐκείνην ἀφῆκά σοι, ἐπεὶ παρεκάλεσάς με·
records.gloss: Then having summoned him the master of him says to him, Slave wicked, all the debt that I forgave you, since you begged me;
pieces: So the master had him called back and said to him, 'Wicked servant! You pleaded with me, and I forgave you the whole of that debt.

L.32: Then his master summoned him and says to him, 'Wicked slave! I forgave you all that debt, because you begged me.

R.32: Then the king called the servant in. He said to him, 'You evil servant! You begged me to help you, so I forgave everything you owed me.

decisions.choice: wicked: evil, here cruel and without mercy
decisions.reason: The word is the usual one for evil. His wickedness is his hardness toward a fellow slave after he had been shown mercy.

decisions.choice: because you begged me: the debt was forgiven only because he asked
decisions.reason: The slave did nothing to earn it. He only asked, and the king forgave.

decisions.choice: present tense of narration (L); past (B, R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the Greek present tense of narration.

decisions.choice: the master's words open here and close at the end of 18:33
alternatives: closing the inner quotation at the end of this sentence
decisions.reason: The master's rebuke runs over two sentences, so the inner quotation stays open.

decisions.choice: to help you
decisions.reason: Readable says what he begged for.

decisions.choice: servant
decisions.reason: "Servant" in Balanced and Readable, as the style guide has it, and Literal keeps "slave".

records.source: οὐκ ἔδει καὶ σὲ ἐλεῆσαι τὸν σύνδουλόν σου, ὡς κἀγὼ σὲ ἠλέησα;
records.gloss: Not was it necessary also you to have mercy on the fellow slave of you, as also I you had mercy?
pieces: Should you not have shown your fellow servant the same mercy I showed you?'

L.33: Should you not also have had mercy on your fellow slave, as I also had mercy on you?'

R.33: You should have shown mercy to the other servant, just as I showed mercy to you.'

decisions.choice: should you not: a question that expects "yes"
decisions.reason: The form expects agreement. He was bound to show the mercy he had received.

decisions.choice: as I had mercy on you: mercy received calls for mercy given
alternatives: mercy as a reward for mercy
decisions.reason: This is the point of the story: those who have been forgiven must forgive. Compare 5:7 and 6:12.

decisions.choice: a statement instead of a question
alternatives: Should you not have had mercy?
decisions.reason: The question expects "yes"; Readable gives the answer.

decisions.choice: servant
decisions.reason: "Servant" in Balanced and Readable, as the style guide has it, and Literal keeps "slave".

records.source: καὶ ὀργισθεὶς ὁ κύριος αὐτοῦ παρέδωκεν αὐτὸν τοῖς βασανισταῖς ἕως οὗ ἀποδῷ πᾶν τὸ ὀφειλόμενον.
records.gloss: And having been angry the master of him handed over him to the torturers until he should pay all the being owed.
pieces: Then the master, now angry, gave him over to the torturers, to stay with them until he had repaid the whole debt.

L.34: And in anger his master handed him over to the torturers until he should pay all that was owed.

R.34: The king was very angry. He handed the servant over to men who would torture him in prison. He would stay there until he paid back everything he owed.

decisions.choice: the torturers: jailers who used torture
decisions.reason: The word means those who torture. Torture was sometimes used on prisoners to make them or their families pay.

decisions.choice: until he should pay all: a debt that could never be paid
decisions.reason: The debt was beyond paying (18:24), so the words point to punishment without release. Jesus applies it in 18:35.

decisions.choice: in anger: the king's anger at the slave's cruelty
decisions.reason: The master was angry because the slave had not shown mercy, not because of the money (18:33).

decisions.choice: men who would torture him in prison
decisions.reason: Readable says who the torturers were.

records.source: Οὕτως καὶ ὁ πατήρ μου ὁ οὐράνιος ποιήσει ὑμῖν ἐὰν μὴ ἀφῆτε ἕκαστος τῷ ἀδελφῷ αὐτοῦ ἀπὸ τῶν καρδιῶν ὑμῶν.
records.gloss: So also the Father of me the heavenly will do to you if not you forgive each the brother of him from the hearts of you.
pieces: My Father in heaven will deal with you in the same way if you do not forgive {{gender:your brother or sister|your brother}} from the heart, each one of you."

L.35: So also {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} heavenly Father will do to you, if you do not each forgive {{gender:your brother or sister|your brother}} from your hearts."

R.35: And {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} Father in heaven will do the same to you if you do not truly forgive {{gender:your brother or sister|your brother}} from your heart."

decisions.choice: so also my Father will do: God will judge the unforgiving
alternatives: God's forgiveness is earned by forgiving others
decisions.reason: As in 6:14-15, forgiveness received and forgiveness given belong together. One who refuses to forgive shows that he has not taken God's mercy to heart.

decisions.choice: from your hearts: truly, from within
decisions.reason: In Scripture the heart is the center of thought and will (5:28). Forgiveness must be real, not only in words.

decisions.choice: brother: a fellow disciple, man or woman
{{gender:your brother or sister|your brother}}
decisions.reason: As in 18:15, the inclusive form is the default.

decisions.choice: the quotation closes here
decisions.reason: The speech that began in 18:22 ends here, and with it the fourth long speech in Matthew. 19:1 returns to the story.

decisions.choice: in heaven
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use the form of 6:9 and 18:10.
